This game is more or less voxel xcom game (meaning you can blow the landscape and buildings up into little cubes). Like xcom, the game is brutally punishing, especially at the start, but as you learn the tricks of this game and gain gear / stats the difficulty begins to even out until you surpass the game. 

A good example is boss fights - every boss fight takes place in a castle map. The first few times you do them, you'll probably go at them like I did room by room and get spanked. Then you start to figure out how to set up good team reaction cover so when you open the door, your team will get some shots off. Then you will figure out how to open up walls with explosives, jumps, or throws. And how to set up a fire trap. Finally towards the end you will simply ambush enemies from the outside by blowing open walls and blasting them with an entire round of salvos all while the ceiling comes raining down on their heads before they even get a turn.

I enjoyed my time with it once I got past the frustrating start and recommend it if your looking for an interesting take on the xcom style.

I've decided its time to update my review.

I love this game, I haven't really played any other turned-based games so I have nothing to compare it to.

Enemy is a rogue-like(ish) RPG game that just combines a bunch of different kinds of fiction together to make this weird but fun mutant thing of a fantasy world. This entire game is trial and error if you don't look at guides like I did, which I don't mind because every failure made me think about new ways to approach enemies and dungeons.

One of the things that makes this game a lot of fun is how much building destruction there is, it's very fun to use the environment to your advantage, ie: blowing a hole in the roof of a dungeon and pouring bullets and grenades down onto my foes. 

I believe they have made the game a bit easier since its release, one of the most useful features is hotels/inns. Whenever you reach a town, there is a hotel which you can spend your gold on to get a checkpoint. Back around this game's release, hotels would only provide you a one time use checkpoint, now you can return to the hotel after an infinite amount of deaths.

Another thing is, whenever a character dies, they are dead for forever unless you saved them at a checkpoint. The first time I finished the game, I probably lost over 20 different characters with somehow keeping the starter character. 

I never felt like the gameplay was mindless, every decision felt strategic. Figuring out how to wisely place and use my characters based off their health, mind, weapons, and skills was a lot of fun. Gold management is also another big thing, whenever you reach a town in this game, you need to choose what would be the best way to spend your gold, "do I get a better weapon? medkits? hotel checkpoint? gun for hire?".

Because everything is based off of chance in this game, there is always a balance between choosing cover or damage, do you want move in for damage? or do you want to stay behind and avoid enemy fire? 

I guess I could go on about this game, but I can't structure reviews very well and I'm pretty stupid.  Either way, if you like RPGs, physics, and strategy, buy this game.

A ideia de Enemy é um jogo de estratégia super complexo, bebendo bastante da fonte do XCom original dos anos 90, com 'time units' e cones de visão e interrupções, mas que acontece com personagems baseados em videogames clássicos dos anos 80. O resultado podia ser babaca, mas não é. É bem divertido dar uma metralhadora para um anjinho e mandar ele atirar em um zumbi. 

Duas das coisas mais interessantes resultam do cenário: a habilidade 'throw', que permite arrancar pedaços do cenário para atirar nos inimigos, e um pulo do Mario que todos os personagens têm, que permite que personagens de longo alcance consigam se posicionar muito bem em cima de árvores, casas e... cogumelos. A única coisa que não casa com o cenário é a 'estabilidade mental' que também é importada dos XCom antigos; já imaginou você ter que parar de jogar Contra porque o seu carinha entrou em pânico depois de testemunhar os horrores da guerra? Além disso, é estranho quando você tem personagens que são guerreiros lendários e androides futuristas e acabam entrando em pânico porque um manezinho do outro lado do nível tá atirando uma pistolinha mais ou menos no mesmo CEP que eles. Não chega a destruir o jogo, mas é um elemento que deixa bem chato.

Outra coisa bem interessante são os cenários destrutíveis. Mas destrutíveis mesmo! Qualquer coisa é feita de blocos e pode ser destruída com ataques. Isso significa que todas as linhas de fogo são reais. Se você atira em um carinha atrás de cobertura, você não ganha -35% na sua rolagem de precisão, você atira mais ou menos na direção dele e pode ser que a bala acerte a cobertura ao invés dele. Você pode destruir telhados e estruturas e derrubar o inimigo de cima delas, ou derrubá-las em cima do inimigo. E com a habilidade 'throw' você pode jogar pedaços do mundo nos inimigos, e dependendo do que você acerta arrancar outros pedaços. É bastante divertido. O único problema é que essa destruição acontece em tempo real, apesar do jogo ser por turnos... às vezes, é possível mover um personagem para fora do caminho de um bólido cadente se for o turno dele. Mas vale a pena pelo que consegue.

O maior problema é que o jogo tem alguns bugs. Já tive um que travou um save - o criador do jogo gentilmente entrou em contato comigo e consertou para mim. Também há alguns menores, como personagens nem sempre conseguindo negociar caminhos que estejam com destroços e a contagem de unidades de tempo ficando completamente louca para personagems que estejam carregando um pedaço do mundo. Geralmente não incomoda, mas como o jogo é um roguelike (bom, tanto quanto XCom eram roguelikes) e também é bastante difícil, há sempre a chance de que uma partida muito boa acabe por causa de um peido digital. A IA também é bem ruizinha; existem ataques 'mágicos' que têm um custo de estabilidade mental, e inimigos vão alegremente usá-los sem parar e entrarem em pânico sozinhos. 

Mas esses são problemas menores para um jogo muito divertido, interessante e diferentão. Altamente recomendo, super divertido, especialmente se você curte os XCom antigos e fica de cara feia com os modernos.

A brutally difficult game that combines the visual aesthetics of Minecraft with the tactical combat of the original X-Com. Default difficulty (which allows achievements) comes with ironman (lack of) saves, so beware!

The plot is short and to the point: the world has been taken over by four boss characters. It’s up to you to stop them.

You start with three characters: two random allies and you, a character who, aside from determining your starting world, and having a blank slate as far as skill points (you have 5 points to assign as you choose), is totally expendable – it’s entirely possible that by the time you get to the second (or even first!) boss that your party will not include any of the original three members.

You’re thrown into combat as soon as you leave your house, and depending on which world you started on (‘platformer’ world - which has giant mushrooms, green pipes, floating treasure boxes, and red brick walls - tends to be the hardest start, with the possibility of spawning living bombs who throw themselves at you, blowing huge chunks out of the area and killing pretty much anything unfortunate enough to be in the blast radius) you may well start losing characters just about immediately.

There are a number of different weapon classes which you can use: various melee weapons, pistols, rifles, bows, crossbows, spells and staffs (which throw out small bomb-like or inferno projectiles), and perhaps my favorite: brute strength, which allows you to rip out chunks of the game world and throw them at your enemies.

And here we come to one of the more fun aspects of ENEMY – the entire world is made up of little cubes, which can (and will) be destroyed in the course of your fighting. Walls will get holes in them, and will eventually buckle; trees will fall down in an explosion of leaf blocks. Trying to get into the boss castle, but the corridor outside the throne room is a deathtrap? Blow a hole in a back wall and go through that way, or if you can make your way up to the roof, toss a bomb and crush everything in a rain of bricks!

Both sounds and music are basic, but serve well enough.

Only two things come to mind as complaints: first that the interface doesn’t seem to have any way to automatically make sure that you hold enough APs in reserve to fire a shot during your interrupt; second is that the game can start to struggle if there are large amounts of bricks falling all at once, as can very well happen in town battles if you (and/or the enemy) use lots of bombs, fire, or staff weapons.

Well worth picking up if any of the above catches your interest.

I really enjoyed playing Enemy. It has its initial premise of course, but it does really well to incorporate the many different weapon types across medieval, modern, and futuristic lines. It also does well to allow the player to employ different strategies to get the job done.

Something I like a lot as well is that you can interact with the terrain or jump on enemies to damage them. Get someone with the Throwing skill to pick up a rock, a metal door, or chunk of wall and just throw it at the enemy. Additionally when you fire off a ranged weapon, watch as you cause pieces of the floor and wall to break off and fall away.

About the only thing I sort of dislike is some of the game's balancing. Lower Level characters seem to be extremely weak compared to Higher Level ones - which is to be expected, but it makes leveling a little too important and that leads to having to farm your character levels. Some enemies also seem to be outright more dangerous then others - going into the Plains for example you can expect to receive a lot of damage.

Part X-Com, Part Rogue-like, and in a world that is fully destructible, Enemy is a fairly unique game all things considered. Perhaps it may inspire other developers to incorporate some of its features. I fully recommend this game.

Only thing I should note is the price of the game - you might want to wait for it to come on sale first before buying it.

A strategically challenging turn-based game on a grid- but with fully 3d destructable environments. I had a blast playing it back when and, having thought of it out of the blue today, I decided to come back and say so!

Simplified XCom/JagAl-like game spiced with destruction. The idea revolves around the risk averse strategies, as any careless move will get your soldiers killed in 1-2 shots. You can't revive them and you can't load game (unless you backup the ..\Documents\enemy). The game saves automatically and you can only save in an inn, but you first need to find the city and get enough money to heal and save. It's not too hard to find new soldiers (squad of 6 max), but you will have to upgrade them from scratch. And their skills let you handle better weapons, first of all. And also run longer, have better accuracy, more health etc.

Metagame is travelling around the map. Environment is quite interesting and some squares have interesting stuff like cities with shops, castles with bosses etc. After clearing the square you can see all the loot in one screen which is very convenient.

Now on the secret sauce - destructible environment. It's not as satisfying as it was done in Silent Storm, but still refreshing. You can shoot through walls, sometimes you miss, but the block goes off and wounds the enemy. And there's a trait which let's you (or enemy) take a block or some bigger elements and through it for damage, which is useful as you won't have too many grenades along the way.

I think TBS fans should try Enemy, at least when discounted. But to put things into a perspective, Xenonauts with a similar price is still better.

+[u]Combat System[/u]: It's sort of like Old-School X-Com where there's a little randomness given to physical shots  but otherwise they do have an effect on the environment (more on this later). There's also an RPG element, your characters level up and you can dump them into various stats, as well as picking up or looting various items, weapons and Armor.

+[u]Theme[/u]: It's basically a tribute to a bunch of old school 80's games mashed into an RPG-Strategy hybrid AND BOY DOES IT WORK! (And it is really funny to see a rifle pop out of a copyright friendly "!" block). Elements from Contra, Mario, Legend of Zelda, Castlevania, Final Fantasy and more are seamlessly integrated in this game and gives it a ton of personality.

+[u]THE PHYSICS ENGINE![/u]: Here's the real star of this game. You see, despite the grid based movement and the number crunching. What really drives everything is an honest to goodness Physics engine, and it makes the game a complete joy to play! I'll list several examples below
[list]
[*] You can pick up and throw LITERALLY ANYTHING and there's even a skill for it! It's actually suprisingly effective, though requires some setup.
[*] Enemies behind a tree? Chop it down by shooting it! In fact the first time I got squadwiped that's what happened! A merc machine gunned a tree down like a bad 80's action movie, killing 2 of my squadmembers (the last one panicked)

[*]Enemy in a building? blow the wall open next to them with a time bomb or a boulder and cave the roof in on them!
[*] Enemy nearby and you think he's going to wreck your squad? Have a guy with some energy saved up jump on him mario style!
[*] Use Melee attacks to shove enemies into things (or off cliffs, in rivers, ect!)

OG Review: If there was an in between option on steam, this would have it. This game is...interesting. Despite what the trailer implies, this is not a fun romp through a sugarcoated wonderland. This game is extremely brutal, and actually VERY dark tone-wise. Unlike XCOM2, there is no overarching grand strategy/research/construction metatgame here. Just a hero you create, two heroes picked from a small pool, and a world that wants you f%cking dead. (The lack of a metagame is a bit of an exaggeration. The metagame is about the brutal scarcity of everything. Shops do not restock, and items and gold in random chests and enemy corpses in the world are rare. This is not to the extent of going to far, though. It's about know what items to use when, and figuring out the best load-outs for your characters from what is available.)

In this game, you kill all the enemies in a region of the map, then move on to the next region, to again, kill everything to advance. Sometimes you will find towns, but everywhere there is a battle to be fought. This may sound repetitive, but isn't. The battlefields are all procedurally generated, and are actually quite well designed at that. (Still agree, even in the same biome the procedural generation is still varied enough to hold my attention after dozens of attempts.)

There is no minimum to how many heros are in your squad. But, every time you go to a new battlefield, it has a random chance of generating a new hero for your squad. The key word, though, is "new." (As in, has full health, but is still on level for were you are in the game, having more skill and having better starting weapons.) On one hand, it is nice that the baddies on the squares on the map that you already beat don't re-spawn, but that also means they won't generate new heroes, either. (Oh, boo hoo.) This becomes problematic, since the areas get harder and harder the further you move from you spawn. (To my past self, caution in this game is a virtue. Not to an unfun degree. Your an inserectionary military squad, not a graoup of suicidal maniacs.) You may simply not have enough manpower to continue. This is compounded by how not only is their permadeath, but it is also absolutely compulsory, due to how the save function was built. (Actually, the post-release update added difficulty levels. On "Normal", you can sleep in an Inn ONCE and create a point to return to if everyone dies, as well as recover some of the squad's health.) 

You may think to yourself, "Oh, so this is kind of like FTL?" No, not really. In FTL, with a bit of luck, you can make it halfway to two/thirds on your first try. But this game is so unforgiving, you will probably die in the first battle if you are not a veteran of tactics games. (Yeah, have experience with the genre will help. However, you will still probably lose in the first or second area. The game is about learning how to get the most out of what you have while learning what tactics are best against each enemies type. Also, you can't play this like XCOM where cover is the end-all be-all, due to the environment being fully destructible and most enemies not using ranged weapons.)

You may think this is a bad game, but is not! It was just made for a very niche audience. If you want a tactics game that takes "easy to learn, difficult to master" to the upmost extreme, this is the game for you. Learning the basic mechanics is very quick. If you want to beat this game, however, prepare to spend a lot of time with it. It is made for a crowd who will pour in hundreds of hours to learn and eventually beat the complexities of the game. If you love tactics games (and I mean really, REALLY love tactics games) and want something you 'can sink you teeth into for months or years, I highly recommend it. If you are just a begginer, or more casual, there are probably better way to spend your time and money. (Yeah, I guess I am not the guy who actually wants to put the time in the beat it. Maybe I'll create a guide when I do.)

Extremely cool game with really satisfying tactical decisions. Reminds me of Jagged Alliance 2 without taking umpteen hours to get anywhere or start doing cool stuff, and without all of the fiddly economic management. Right from the jump, you'll be: accidentally bulldozing walls, knocking trees over onto enemies, starting uncontrollable fires that threaten to engulf everything you hold near and dear, and assessing every map for every exploitable tactic you can muster in an effort to keep your squad alive as the world starts scaling beyond what your six-person squad can honorably annihilate. The game gets tense as hell, as the intended play mode is essentially Iron Man mode in a world with dwindling resources. There's an easier mode with saves and less dwindling, but fie on that.

In a lot of ways, it's an ingeniously modernized X-Com 1/2 or JA2, in that it strips out all of the base-building and research and economic worrying, reinvests some of that into character leveling, simplifies the controls to what are actually necessary, adds genuinely destructible terrain and structures with good physics and fire modeling, and makes the time between booting the game for the first time and doing something fun about 2 minutes; and it does all this while still retaining the fundamental complexity of the squad tactics in X-Com/JA2. 

An unkind reviewer would say it's JA2-lite, which is true in a sense, but I don't have a problem with that. I'm not trying to spend 200+ hours fomenting a revolution again; I'm just trying to sledgehammer someone into and through a wall.

Also, surprisingly good music, sfx and cryptic NPC dialogues.

Enemy is a turn based RPG with a few interesting differences.

First of all, you create your own character, then gather additional party members as you play, until you reach the maximum party size of 6. The characters are all based on common gaming characters - the action hero (good with guns) the wizard (focuses on staff weapons) and so on.

You move your characters, then the computer moves theirs. The goal is to kill all the enemies in the area, then move on. There are zone bosses to kill, and once you have defeated them all (there are currently 4) you win.

There are elements of roguelikes here too - permadeath for characters, and while the game autosaves fairly often, you can't save-scum and reload. Decisions are final.

What makes this special, for me, is the physics. Everything is destructable, and it is endlessly entertaining watching a stray shot bring down a tree that flattens an enemy, or making a tactful decision to blow up a buildings weak points in order to make it collapse in on the occupants. Fire spreads and degrades the materials it touches, and weakens them.

The AI is fairly basic, the challenge lies in being prepared for surprise attacks and not letting yourself be pinned into a situation you can't get out of. The game is pretty hard at first, but once you get the hang of it, and gather some extra party members, it gets easier... until you find yourself trying to kill an undead vampire lord with 6 allies of his own in a close-quarters battle-royale in a crumbling and fragile stone castle ...... and you've only got an explosive throwing lunatic as your available character.


I highly recommend it.

So, this one is a pretty interesting game, conceptually.  It has alot of things going for it.  It's a tactical squad strategy game, which reminds me alot of Silent Storm, actually.  And clearly takes some inspiration from the old Xcom games.

There's alot going on here; you've got randomly generated maps, a big worldmap to explore, towns to go to and buy stuff in, characters to recruit, and a wonderful destructible landscape.  It's very satisfying to watch things shatter when they are hit, and every individual brick or block or whatever is a seperate entity, and can collide with and injure characters.   There's tons of different weapons and items, an easy to use level-up-your-skills sort of thing, and of course permadeath.

But, there's one thing that, for me, absolutely grinds this all to a halt and keeps it from meeting, or even getting close, to it's potential, and that's the morale system, if that's the correct word.

Every character, friend or foe, has a stat representing their mind/morale/courage.  When enemy attacks are fired at your characters, they'll take a hit to this number... no matter if the attack misses or hits them.  When this drops to zero, they will flip the hell out, and either run around like utter morons (problem number 1) or go berserk.  The running around bit is a problem because it DOESNT MAKE ANY SENSE.  I understand the idea of representing a "fight or flight" response, and the urge to get the hell out of there to save yourself.   Too bad it's so poorly implemented though. Your characters wont run AWAY from the enemy; they'll simply run in totally random directions for awhile.  And I mean TOTALLY random.  They absolutely will end up standing 5 blocks away from 2 guys with shotguns and a ninja, or just stand in an open field with snipers everywhere, or.... you get the idea.  This makes no sense at all.  These guys, if they're going to panic, should run AWAY from the enemy.  You know, like people would actually do.  You run AWAY from the threat.  Not just zoom around in different directions followed by shoving your nose up the barrel of some guy's gun.  They can also go berserk instead, at which point they'll try a desperate attack against an enemy, and this one DOES actually work like it sounds, and so isnt much of a problem.

But then there's the way the whole thing is activated.  As I said, when attacked, your guys will get more and more scared.  But here's the thing:  they'll get freaked out EVEN IF IT MAKES NO SENSE.  If they're up against some guy who is so fantastically stupid that he's on the other side of the map, fires a gun DIRECTLY at a heavy object that's RIGHT in front of him, and thus hits it, your guys, who again are on the OTHER SIDE OF THE MAP, will stand there and go "HOLY EXPLODING COWS, BATMAN!!! That one almost hit me square in the forehead!  What a deadly sniper that guy is! I better get away!".  They will do this every.  Single.  Time.  And believe me, it gets really old, really fast.  You end up having to come up with somewhat odd tactics JUST to deal with something that is basically broken from the start.  Not a good thing, and for me, even though I wasnt exactly dying much, it just got so damn stupid that my interest just shattered.  Even if I won the map, I was like "That.... that was just so dumb.  I had to change my strategy because the bad guy pretty much shot himself in the foot a mile away, causing my idiot melee guy to run into the open and do a little dance for no reason!" and.... yeah.  I was just done at that point.   I love strategy games, normally.  But when they hit a point where logic just goes completely out the window, I just lose interest.

And that's pretty much what happened with this one.   Being totally honest, I dont think that mechanic is even necessary.  Particularly considering the theme behind the game.  Your guy isnt just some random idiot; he's clearly an adventurer, having already been on assorted game-ish quests, like being a horror game protagonist, to hopping over spikes and into pipes like Mario.  The pathetic reactions to.... basically everything.... just dont make sense in this context.   I can understand a mechanic like that being added to up the difficulty.  But there's SO many other ways to add extra challenge without having to resort to something like that, as so very many other games have proven already.  

All in all, it's not a bad game, but just has some glaring flaws (as that's not the only odd issue it has) that for some players might ruin it entirely.  I strongly suggest watching some videos and lets' plays on the game before buying, to get a sense of how it works. 

For now though, I cant entirely recommend it myself.  But your tastes may definitely differ from mine.  Again, it's not bad. But particularly when compared to so many other strategy games out there, it just doesnt quite hit the point where I can genuinely give it a positive score here.

Honestly, I'd rather give it a more neutral score, but Steam's overly simplistic system here doesnt allow me to say "Well, considering everything, I think this is a 6 out of 10, it's a decent game and you might like it but there's definitely some big issues". And I do still play it.  But since I cant just outright recommend the game and am suggesting that people watch some of it for awhile before buying, I'm not giving a thumbs up here.

[list]

[*] Despite the fact that you can stomp mechants who charge you outrageous prices, you cannot loot their steel chests for their wares. Of course, the huge box [i]can[/i] be used to completely demolish the side of the hotel when that greedy concierge works.
[*] P.R.I.N.C.E.S.S. stands for: "Person Reprogrammed to Immediately Neutralize Castles by Excessively Slinging Stuff."

Kind of like the movie 'The Wickerman', only that he'll be burning like wicker, man.

[*] Despite interrupting an Explod'steve in mid jump with a ranged character, you can still miss even with 60%-70% accuracy, often with humorous/frustrating results. This happened to me twice within the same playthrough. Needlessly to say, I didn't get lucky twice.
